name: Consortium Governance
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Who's In Charge When No One's In Charge: Designing Consortium Governance
lesson.summary: A consortium blockchain replaces one company's IT department with a shared system run by rivals and partners, so its rules for membership, voting, and dispute resolution matter as much as its code.
lesson.body:
A consortium blockchain, as defined earlier in this course, is run by a fixed, known set of organizations rather than one company or an open, anonymous crowd. That single fact changes almost everything about how the system has to be run. A public company can change its own internal database schema on a Tuesday afternoon because it owns the database. A consortium of a dozen banks, shippers, or hospitals cannot, because no single member owns the shared infrastructure, yet every member depends on it. Governance is the name for the rules and bodies that answer the questions a normal IT department would just decide unilaterally: who may join, who may be removed, how upgrades are approved, how costs are split, and who resolves a dispute when two members disagree about what the ledger should say.

Concretely, a well-designed consortium usually separates governance into layers. A steering committee, often with a rotating chair so no single member can dominate indefinitely, sets strategic direction and approves major changes such as admitting a new member or amending the consortium's operating agreement. A technical working group, staffed by engineers from member organizations, proposes and reviews smart contract upgrades or protocol changes, which typically require a supermajority vote rather than unanimity, since requiring every single member to agree tends to freeze the network the first time two competitors disagree. An admissions process vets prospective members not just technically but on know-your-customer and anti-money-laundering grounds, since adding a member to a shared ledger is closer to admitting a partner than installing a plugin. Because there is no central authority to sue the way you might sue a single vendor, the operating agreement usually specifies arbitration or another dispute resolution mechanism up front.

The stakes of getting this wrong are not hypothetical. TradeLens, a shipping and logistics consortium platform built by Maersk and IBM, is a widely discussed case: the underlying technology worked, and the platform onboarded a meaningful set of ocean carriers, ports, and customs authorities, yet it was shut down in 2022. A large part of the reason was governance and trust, not code: rival shipping lines were reluctant to route their competitive data through infrastructure that was co-owned by one of their direct competitors, no matter how the smart contracts were written. A technically sound consortium chain still needs governance that convinces rivals the shared infrastructure will treat them fairly, and no amount of cryptography substitutes for that.

This is why consortium governance deserves its own chapter distinct from the general idea of governance you saw earlier in the course. General blockchain governance asks how a protocol evolves over time. Consortium governance asks something narrower and more organizationally loaded: how do a handful of parties who may be commercial rivals, who all have veto-relevant leverage because the network needs their participation to be useful, agree to share infrastructure at all. Voting weight is a good place to see this tension directly. Should each member get one vote regardless of size, protecting smaller participants from being steamrolled? Or should votes be weighted by transaction volume or capital contributed, rewarding the members who have the most to lose? Neither answer is objectively correct; the right one depends on what the consortium is trying to build trust around, and getting it wrong is a governance failure long before it becomes a technical one.
